issues.legal_issue: A will is proved when its execution is established and genuine, material suspicions are dispelled; excluding natural heirs, without more, does not make it suspicious.
material_facts: The testatrix executed and registered a will leaving the disputed property to one daughter, who had been widowed young, had lived with her mother for more than twenty years, and had cared for her.
The other daughters lived with their husbands elsewhere, and there was no evidence that the beneficiary received support from her late husband's family.
One attesting witness testified to the will, and the court found no defect in his testimony.
The testatrix personally attended the registration office and died several years after executing the will.
There was no evidence that the testatrix suffered from an ailment impairing her mental faculties when she executed the will.
The lower courts treated the exclusion of the other daughters, the testatrix's physical limitations, and the non-examination of the typist and an advocate as grounds for rejecting the will.
issues.conclusion: The will was genuine. The exclusion of the other daughters was not, in these circumstances, a sufficient ground to doubt its authenticity, and the beneficiary's testimony from one attesting witness satisfied the applicable proof requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be signed or marked by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses in the prescribed manner; Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, requires examination of an attesting witness, and its proviso permits proof by one attesting witness where applicable. The propounder bears the burden of proving the will and, where real suspicious circumstances arise, explaining them to the court's satisfaction; allegations of fraud, coercion, or undue influence must be proved by the person making them. Exclusion or reduced provision for natural heirs alone is not a suspicious circumstance, since a will alters the normal course of succession. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, PPK Gopalan Nambiar v. PPK Balakrishan Manbiar, Pushpavati v. Chandraja Kadamba, and Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee.

rule.if: will_based_property_suit and attesting_witness_examined and (beneficiary_was_dependent_caregiver or exclusion_was_only_suspicion) and no_evidence_of_testator_mental_incapacity

predicates.will_based_property_suit: A civil property proceeding depends on whether a will is genuine.
predicates.attesting_witness_examined: The party propounding the will examined an attesting witness who testified to its execution, and the testimony was not found defective.
predicates.beneficiary_was_dependent_caregiver: The will benefited a person who depended on the testator and had cared for the testator over a substantial period.
predicates.exclusion_was_only_suspicion: The exclusion or reduced provision for natural heirs was the sole substantive ground for treating the will as suspicious.
predicates.no_evidence_of_testator_mental_incapacit: The opposing party produced no evidence that the testator's mental faculties were impaired when the will was executed.

issues.definition: When a will-based property suit includes proof by an attesting witness and the beneficiary's caregiving or the exclusion of heirs explains the disposition, and there is no evidence of the testator's mental incapacity, the will is accepted as genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A testamentary beneficiary takes only the share that the testator inherited where the testator's spouse and daughters succeeded equally to the estate of a male who died intestate after the applicable succession law took effect.
material_facts: The disputed property had belonged to the deceased father, who died after the Hindu Succession Act had come into force.
His surviving heirs included his widow and seven daughters.
The mother therefore inherited only an equal share with the other heirs, and her will could pass only the share she owned.
issues.conclusion: The mother owned only one-eighth of the estate, and the beneficiary took that share under the will in addition to her own share.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and held that, because the deceased father died after the Act came into force, his widow and daughters succeeded equally. The judgment does not identify a particular section or rely on an earlier case for this determination.

rule.if: male_intestate_succession_case and succession_law_was_in_force_at_death and widow_and_daughters_survived and will_transferred_testatrix_interest

predicates.male_intestate_succession_case: The proceeding concerns succession to the estate of a male who died without a will governing that estate.
predicates.succession_law_was_in_force_at_death: The applicable succession law was in force when the deceased died.
predicates.widow_and_daughters_survived: The deceased was survived by a widow and daughters who succeeded to the estate.
predicates.will_transferred_testatrix_interest: A later will purports to transfer property that the testator inherited from the deceased.

issues.definition: When a male intestate dies while the applicable succession law is in force and is survived by a widow and daughters, a beneficiary under the widow's later will takes only the widow's inherited share.
